title: Development and validation of an interpretable Random Forest model for predicting recurrence after endoscopic submucosal dissection in superficial oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma

paragraphs.en: Oesophageal cancer is a prevalent malignancy with high incidence and mortality rates worldwide [1]. The two main subtypes of oesophageal cancer are squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma, and there are marked geographical variations in their distribution. China has a high incidence of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) [2]. Due to absence of typical symptoms in the early stages, many patients have entered the middle and late stages when diagnosed, leading to poor overall prognosis and a five-year survival rate of less than 30% [3]. Studies have shown that after endoscopic or surgical treatment of oesophageal cancer in the early stage, the five-year survival rate can reach 95% [4]. Therefore, improving the early diagnosis rate of oesophageal cancer and implementing timely treatment can contribute to improve patient prognosis. Superficial oesophageal squamous carcinoma (SESCC) refers to oesophageal cancer confined to the oesophageal mucosa or submucosa. In recent years, the popularization of endoscopic screening technology and the application of high-resolution imaging technologies have significantly improved the detection rate of SESCC, providing an important window period for minimally invasive treatment.

Compared with traditional surgical radical resection of oesophageal cancer, endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) has become the first-line treatment option for SESCC due to its minimally invasive nature, low complication rate and comparable efficacy to preserve organ functions. A meta-analysis pointed out that compared with radical resection of oesophageal cancer, ESD did not show significant differences in treatment effectiveness and had a lower incidence of adverse events [5]. However, due to background mucosa remains after ESD, some patients with superficial oesophageal cancer still have the risk of postoperative recurrence and may require multiple resection or additional chemoradiotherapy, which may prolong the treatment cycle and increase the consumption of medical resources. Studies reported that the recurrence rate after ESD fluctuates between 0.55% and 15.38% [6]. Therefore, identifying risk factors related to postoperative recurrence of ESD plays an important role in optimizing treatment options and improving treatment outcomes.

In recent years, most relevant literature reports have focused on the study of complications associated with ESD treatment for SESCC, while there have been few reports on exploring the risk factors associated with local recurrence or metachronous recurrence after ESD. In addition, the assessment of post-ESD recurrence risk mostly relies on nomogram models constructed by traditional statistical methods, but it is limited by stringent data structure requirements and is difficult to fully capture the nonlinear interactions of multi-dimensional risk factors. Machine learning algorithms are being widely used in clinical practice, covering areas such as disease diagnosis, treatment risk assessment and medical data analysis [7,8]. Unlike traditional analysis methods used in previous research, machine learning has significant advantages in processing large data sets and exploring nonlinear relationships [9]. It can optimize variable weight allocation through feature selection and integration of high-dimensional data; reduce the risk of overfitting through cross-validation and integration learning; and support dynamic updates to adapt to time-series changes in clinical data. However, there have been no studies to build a machine learning prediction model for post-ESD recurrence of SESCC. Therefore, this study was designed to use machine learning algorithms to build a high-precision and interpretable prediction model and provide new tools for individualized recurrence prediction and treatment decision-making, to improve patient outcomes.

This study retrospectively collected patients with SESCC who received ESD treatment at the Endoscopy Center of the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University from 1 January 2016 to 31 December 2023. We included the patients with the following criteria: (1) Initial ESD treatment; (2) SESCC was confirmed by postoperative pathology; (3) Complete medical record information and endoscopic treatment data; (4) Follow-up time exceeded six months. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Patients who were not undergoing ESD treatment for the first time; (2) Patients who underwent endoscopic surgery other than ESD for the first time; (3) Patients who had undergone surgical oesophagectomy or other anti-tumour therapies before or after ESD;(4) Patients with other malignancies were excluded; (5) Patients with incomplete clinical data or lost to follow-up after ESD. This retrospective study was approved by the Ethics Committee and Review Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (2024-SR-499), and all patients provided written informed consent before receiving ESD treatment. The flow chart of this study is shown in Figure 1.

We reviewed medical records to gather clinical traits and surgical data: (1) demographic characteristics, such as age, gender, smoking history, drinking history and family history and (2) preoperative blood test indicators, including routine blood tests and biochemical indicators. According to the data preprocessing, the relevant indicators reflecting the inflammatory, nutritional and ageing status of individuals were included, such as neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), neutrophil percentage-albumin ratio (NPAR) and biological age (BA). NLR was defined as absolute neutrophil count divided by absolute lymphocyte count. LMR was defined as absolute lymphocyte counts divided by absolute monocyte count. PLR was defined as absolute platelet counts divided by absolute lymphocyte count. NPAR was calculated as follows: neutrophil percentage(%) × 100/albumin concentration(g/dL). (3) Tumour characteristics, including location, size, number, invasion depth, tumour differentiation and complete resection. Complete resection was defined as no tumour residue at the lateral and basal margins of the endoscopically resected specimen.

Patients meeting the inclusion criteria were followed up at least every six months in the first year after ESD and once a year thereafter. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was reviewed to record the patient’s survival status and recurrence during the follow-up period. The aim of this study was to build a model that can predict occurrence rather than timing of recurrence in patients after ESD. The diagnosis of recurrence is mainly based on relevant pathological examinations, including local recurrence and metachronous multiple primary oesophageal cancer. Local recurrence is defined as the discovery of cancer cells at the original resection site and within 1 cm on follow-up endoscopy six months after ESD treatment. Metachronous multiple primary oesophageal cancer refers to the occurrence of a new oesophageal cancer lesion beyond 1 cm from the original resection site more than 12 months after endoscopic treatment.

This study estimates biological age by integrating mathematical modelling methods of multidimensional biomarkers. Through a systematic review of computational methods in related literature, we selected 28 representative candidate biomarkers based on three factors: the existing research foundation, applications in prior ageing studies and the availability of the dataset in this study. In this study, the Klemera-Doubal method (KDM) is used to compute biological age [10–12]. Specifically, we calculated the correlation coefficients between each biomarker and chronological age (CA) and selected biomarkers with coefficients higher than 0.10 to build the KDM-BA model. Notably, during the initial screening, a high correlation (r > .7) was found between red blood cell count (RBC) and haemoglobin (Hb) [11]. Based on the calculated correlation coefficients, RBC was retained as a representative indicator in the final model. Subsequently, biomarkers were stratified by gender, and principal component analysis (PCA) based on the correlation matrix was used to transform the selected biomarkers into principal components (PCs). Then, KDM-BA was calculated using Klemera and Doubal’s formula. The calculation formula is as follows:
m: the number of principal components (PCs);
xj: the jth PC;
qj: the intercept of the regression of jth PC on BA, since BA is unknown, it is replaced by CA, the same as below;
kj: the slope of the regression of jth PC on BA;
sj: the root mean square error of the regression of jth PC on BA;
sBA: the root mean square error of the regression of CA on BA, and it can be replaced by the root mean square error of the regression of all PCs on CA account of unknown BA.

All laboratory indicators remained continuous and were not classified. Classification predictors were defined prior to model construction. The data for categorical variables were processed using a one-hot encoding method. To prevent data leakage, the data preprocessing steps were applied separately to the training set and the temporal validation set. Missing data were processed using the ‘mice’ package in R software for chain equation multiple interpolation. Based on the data distribution map before/after imputation, the consistency of distribution between the estimated data and the raw data was assessed to ensure validity. Random errors and model uncertainties are combined to finally integrate the imputation results through statistical analysis. Strictly separate the pre-processing pipeline of training and time-validated sets to prevent data leakage.

In this study, we utilized recursive feature elimination (RFE) alongside the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression to select key predictive factors. RFE is a widely used feature selection method in machine learning that eliminates irrelevant features to derive an optimal feature subset, simplifying the model and enhancing its interpretability, which is beneficial for clinical applications [13]. We implemented ten-fold cross-validation during the RFE process to evaluate model performance, reinforcing the reliability of variable selection and model generalization. LASSO regression effectively removes variables that are either irrelevant to model prediction or exhibit multicollinearity, thereby achieving dimensionality reduction and feature selection [14].

We designated individuals enrolled between January 2016 and December 2021 as the training set and split it in a 7:3 ratio for model training and internal validation randomly. To further assess model performance, patients enrolled between January 2022 and December 2023 were used as the temporal validation set. The Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) algorithm was applied in the training set to address the issue of class imbalance. As an advanced preprocessing method for imbalanced data, SMOTE identifies neighbouring samples for minority-class instances using the k-nearest neighbours algorithm and synthesizes new samples via linear random interpolation [15]. Subsequently, seven machine learning algorithms were employed to construct risk models: logistic regression (LR), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM), random forest (RF), gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT), Gaussian Naïve Bayes (GNB) and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). Ten-fold cross-validation combined with the default hyperparameter grid search in the ‘caret’ package was used to determine the optimal hyperparameters for each model, ensuring model stability and reproducibility.

The area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) served as the primary statistical criterion for selecting the best-performing machine learning model, while accuracy, sensitivity, positive predictive value (PPV), F1-score and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) were used to comprehensively assess model performance. The closer these statistical metrics are to 1, the better the model’s predictive performance. The DeLong test was employed to determine whether there was a significant difference in the AUC values of different models [16]. Additionally, calibration curves were employed to evaluate how well the predicted probabilities aligned with the observed results. Decision curve analysis (DCA) was performed to effectively evaluate the clinical utility of the model in real-world decision-making. We employed the Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) approach to elucidate the predictive model, providing insight into the influence of individual variables on outcomes [17]. As a game theory-based method, SHAP enables interpretation at both the individual prediction level and the overall model level, improving transparency and interpretability [18]. To facilitate the application of the model by clinicians, researchers, patients and their families, the final predictive model was integrated into a web-based platform developed using the Shiny application. Users can obtain predictive results simply by entering relevant clinical parameters on the web interface.

Data analysis and visualization in this study were conducted using R software (version 4.3.1) and Shiny (version 1.10.0). Continuous variables were summarized using the median and interquartile range (IQR) and comparisons between two groups were performed using the Mann-Whitney rank-sum test. Categorical variables were assessed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, with results presented as frequencies and percentages. The identification of risk factors across the entire cohort (training and temporal validation sets) was conducted using univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses. A restricted cubic spline (RCS) function was used to evaluate the dose-response relationship between independent risk factors and recurrence. Statistical significance was defined as a p value <.05.

A total of 794 patients were enrolled in this retrospective study. Among them, 112 patients (14.1%) developed postoperative recurrence. Table 1 summarizes the demographic and clinicopathological characteristics of all patients. Compared with the non-recurrence group, the recurrence group had a higher proportion of poorly differentiated tumours (31.3% vs. 21.6%) and multiple lesions (27.7% vs. 14.5%), while the complete resection rate was lower (72.3% vs. 79.3%). The recurrence group had higher levels of albumin (ALB) and fasting blood glucose (FBG) compared to the non-recurrence group (ALB: 40.4 vs. 39.8, FBG: 4.89 vs. 4.77), whereas their LMR and BA were significantly lower (LMR: 3.88 vs. 4.44, BA: 62 ± 9 vs. 65 ± 11). As shown in Supplementary Table S1, baseline characteristics were comparable between the training and temporal validation cohorts.

Supplementary Table S2 shows the distribution of 8 blood biomarkers used to calculate BA in the recurrence and non-recurrence groups, including lymphocyte count (LYC), RBC, mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration (MCHC), red blood cell distribution width coefficient of variation (RDW-CV), monocyte percentage (MONO%), albumin (ALB), retinol-binding protein (RBP) and adenosine deaminase (ADA). In the overall study population, BA ranged from 21 to 103 years, with a mean of 64 years (SD = 11). In the recurrence group, BA ranged from 40 to 93 years, with a mean of 62 years (SD = 9). In the non-recurrence group, BA ranged from 21 to 103 years, with a mean of 65 years (SD = 11). The BA in the recurrence group was significantly lower than that in the non-recurrence group (p = .005). Supplementary Figure S1 showed that KDM-BA was highly correlated with chronological age (CA) (cor = 0.71). Furthermore, to improve accessibility, we incorporated the BA calculation process into an online platform for clinical use. By inputting the relevant feature data on the webpage, users can instantly retrieve their BA. The web application is accessible at: https://zzhapp.shinyapps.io/bashiny/ (Supplementary Figure S2).

We analysed the independent risk factors contributing to postoperative recurrence in SESCC patients using data from the entire study cohort. Consequently, univariate analysis identified five significant predictors that were strongly correlated with postoperative recurrence (p < .05). Further multivariate logistic regression analysis confirmed four independent predictors of postoperative recurrence in SESCC patients: tumour differentiation, number of lesions, LMR and FBG (p < .05) (Supplementary Table S3).

Based on the results of multivariate logistic regression, we further examined the associations of LMR and FBG levels with postoperative recurrence in SESCC patients. Prior to the dose-response analysis, we adjusted for confounding factors and utilized the restricted cubic spline (RCS) method to assess nonlinearity [19]. Notably, although BA was not independently associated with postoperative recurrence risk in SESCC patients (p = .082), its confidence interval remained within a potentially relevant range (0.96–1.00). Consequently, BA was also evaluated for nonlinearity. As illustrated in the dose-response curve (Figure 2), BA exhibited a nonlinear association with postoperative recurrence in SESCC patients (overall p < .05, nonlinearity p < .05). For patients with a BA of less than 60.84 years, postoperative recurrence risk increased gradually as BA rose. Conversely, for patients with a BA greater than 60.84 years, the risk of recurrence declined sharply. Additionally, neither LMR nor FBG levels demonstrated a significant overall or nonlinear association with postoperative recurrence in SESCC patients (overall p > .05, nonlinearity p > .05).

We utilized the RFE algorithm along with LASSO regression for feature selection (Figure 3). Finally, a total of eight selected features were ultimately selected for developing a risk prediction model for postoperative recurrence in SESCC patients. These features included PLR, LMR, LDL, BA, tumour location, number of lesions, tumour differentiation and infiltration depth (Supplementary Figure S3).

The selected features were utilized for model training and validation. Performance evaluation on the internal test set (Figure 4) showed that all seven machine learning models (LR, XGBoost, LightGBM, RF, GBDT, GNB and MLP) exhibited strong discriminative ability, with AUC (95% CI) values of 0.666 (0.548–0.784), 0.865 (0.785–0.946), 0.747 (0.636–0.858), 0.892 (0.818–0.965), 0.855 (0.771–0.939), 0.688 (0.573–0.803) and 0.583 (0.459–0.707), respectively. Table 2 compares key performance metrics across the seven machine learning models. Based on the comprehensive performance evaluation, the RF model demonstrated superior predictive ability for recurrence risk, with the highest accuracy (0.823 [0.795–0.851]), specificity (0.948 [0.926–0.969]), positive predictive value (PPV) (0.914 [95% CI 0.879–0.949]) and F1-score (0.77 [95% CI 0.729–0.811]). Additionally, precision-recall curve analysis (Figure 4) demonstrated that the RF model achieved the highest area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) in the internal test set, reaching 0.905 (95% CI 0.883–0.927). The DeLong test showed that the AUC of the RF model was higher than that of several other models, and the differences were statistically significant (p < .05) (Supplementary Table S4). The calibration curve indicated that the RF model exhibited the highest calibration performance, with a calibration score of 0.125 (95% CI: 0.112–0.138). Decision curve analysis (DCA) indicated that the RF model outperformed all others across the full threshold range (0.2–0.8), with the XGBoost model ranking second. Overall, the RF model was identified as the optimal approach for risk prediction. To assess its generalizability, the trained RF model was temporally validated, yielding an AUC of 0.761 (95% CI: 0.659–0.863), confirming its robustness (Figure 5). Supplementary Table 5 shows the hyperparameters for the seven models.

sections.title: SHAP interpretability in the predictive model

paragraphs.en: The SHAP method was utilized to explain the predictions of the final model by assessing the contribution of each variable to the outcome. This interpretability approach offers two levels of explanation: global interpretation at the feature level and local interpretation at the individual level. Global interpretation provides insights into the model’s general decision-making process. The SHAP summary bar plot (Figure 6(A)) ranks features by their mean SHAP values, highlighting the top five key predictors: number of lesions, tumour location, tumour differentiation, LMR and LDL. The SHAP dot plot (Figure 6(B)) intuitively illustrates how each feature influences model predictions: multiple tumour lesions, poor differentiation and elevated LDL and PLR values increased recurrence risk, while mid-oesophageal tumour location and higher BA were protective factors. Moreover, local interpretation reveals how individual predictions are made by quantifying and displaying the influence of each feature on a specific sample. The SHAP waterfall plot (Figure 6(C)) demonstrates how each feature, through its specific value and corresponding SHAP score, contributes positively or negatively to predicting recurrence in the second SESCC patient. Multiple tumour lesions, poor differentiation, BA level of 57.5 and tumour invasion depth reaching M3 or SM1 contributed significantly to the prediction, with SHAP values of +0.22, +0.0788, +0.0552 and +0.0458, respectively. Other features, such as LDL, PLR and tumour location in the mid-oesophagus, also had varying levels of influence. The final model predicted that this patient belonged to the postoperative recurrence group, aligning with the actual outcome. The waterfall plot offers deeper insights into the model’s decision-making mechanism.

Figure 7 shows that the final predictive model was integrated into an online platform for clinical application (Supplementary Deployment Guide). By entering the necessary clinical features into the web-based interface, users can obtain an automated prediction of postoperative recurrence risk. The predictive tool is available online at: https://zzhapp.shinyapps.io/shiny/.

Current research on recurrence following ESD for SESCC primarily focuses on exploring risk factors and developing predictive models based on traditional statistical methods. For instance, Ruan et al. and Wang et al. used logistic regression to create nomograms predicting lymph node metastasis in SESCC patients post-surgery, focusing on pathological features like tumour invasion depth, differentiation degree and lymphovascular invasion [20,21]. While these models demonstrated AUC values exceeding 0.75, which offer valuable insights for clinical practice, their applicability is constrained to surgical cohorts. Consequently, they may not adequately address the need for effective recurrence risk management following ESD. Our study goes beyond the limitations of traditional statistical frameworks by developing an interpretable predictive model to assess the risk of recurrence in SESCC patients after ESD treatment and systematically validating the model’s performance. To our knowledge, this may be one of the few existing tools for predicting recurrence risk in SESCC patients following ESD treatment. Compared to previous conventional models, this study exhibits several innovative aspects. First, by systematically evaluating seven different machine learning algorithms, we moved beyond the limitations of single-algorithm applications and further validated the model’s temporal generalizability using a 2022–2023 dataset as a temporal validation cohort. The results demonstrate that the RF model outperformed others in this rigorous comparison, leveraging its inherent strengths to identify complex nonlinear interactions among predictive variables [22–25]. Second, we expanded the feature set beyond traditional pathological indicators by integrating systemic inflammatory markers, metabolic parameters and the novel concept of biological age, thereby achieving a more comprehensive risk assessment. Furthermore, in this study, we applied multivariate logistic regression to identify independent risk factors and employed the RFE-LASSO method for feature selection. The integration of these two methodologies facilitates a more nuanced understanding of individual predictors. A pertinent illustration of this is fasting blood glucose (FBG). Although multivariate logistic regression identified FBG as an independent risk factor, it was not included in the final model as determined by the RFE-LASSO algorithm. This is not a contradiction but rather reflects the complementary nature of the two methods: logistic regression identifies statistically significant associations, while the machine learning–based method optimizes predictive simplicity by systematically excluding variables that contain redundant information within the extensive feature set. Through the RFE-LASSO algorithm, we ultimately identified eight key features, effectively addressing issues of multicollinearity and overfitting in high-dimensional data. Finally, we deployed the final model on an online prediction platform for clinicians, clinical researchers and patients to support shared decision-making and optimize follow-up resource allocation.

To improve model transparency, this study used the SHAP method to analyse the impact of key predictive factors on the outcome. The final model included eight variables: number of lesions, tumour location, tumour differentiation, LMR, LDL, BA, PLR and invasion depth. The SHAP analysis positioned the number of lesions as the most influential predictor overall, a finding that was strongly corroborated by multivariate logistic regression, which identified multiple lesions as an independent risk factor conferring a 2.31-fold higher recurrence risk (OR = 2.31, 95% CI 1.44–3.72, p < .001). Multiple studies show that multiple Lugol’s voiding lesions (LVLs) are significantly associated with an increased risk of recurrence in SESCC patients after ESD and that the Lugol’s staining pattern can serve as an effective stratification tool for the risk of metachronous recurrence [6]. Similarly, the association of poor differentiation with higher recurrence risk, consistent with its known link to lymph node metastasis, was affirmed by both its significant odds ratio and high mean SHAP value [26–29]. In addition, deeper invasion to the submucosal superficial layer increases the risk of postoperative recurrence. This finding aligns with prior research indicating that in early oesophageal cancer patients treated with ESD, tumours with primary lesions invading the submucosal layer are more prone to lymph node metastasis [30,31].

In recent years, the significance of preoperative inflammatory markers in tumour prognosis assessment has increasingly attracted attention. NLR, LMR and PLR reflect the balance between pro-cancer inflammatory responses and anti-cancer immune modulation. The LMR was affirmed as a key predictor by both methods, being an independent risk factor in logistic regression and a top-five contributor in the SHAP summary. Lowered LMR may influence the recurrence risk through several mechanisms: reduced LMR is often accompanied by lymphocytopenia, which leads to impaired tumour cell clearance and immune surveillance, thereby preventing the effective elimination of residual micro-lesions post-surgery [32–36]. The inclusion of PLR in the final model, alongside LMR, underscores the composite information conveyed by systemic inflammation. Notably, the global interpretation indicates that patients with higher LDL levels are more prone to postoperative recurrence. This finding raises the hypothesis that LDL-lowering interventions might contribute to reducing postoperative recurrence risk, which aligns with emerging evidence linking dyslipidemia to tumour progression [37]. Most notably, the role of Biological Age (BA) demonstrated the unique power of machine learning to capture complex, non-linear relationships. Although BA did not reach statistical independence (p = .082), its prominent role in the RF model and the U-shaped dose-response curve indicates that recurrence risk increases with BA in younger patients but decreases in older cohorts (inflection point at 60.84 years). Conversely, the sharp decline in risk for older patients could be associated with less aggressive tumour behaviour, immune microenvironment characteristics and stricter surgical eligibility criteria, supported by observations of enhanced immune responses in elderly cohorts [38,39]. Clinical follow-up should be adjusted according to age: younger patients should have shorter follow-up intervals, and high-resolution endoscopy can be used to monitor small lesions.

Nevertheless, this study has some unavoidable limitations. Firstly, as the data is from a single-centre retrospective cohort, selection bias may be present. Secondly, the exclusion of novel biomarkers such as radiomics features or molecular markers may limit further improvements in model performance. Finally, we evaluated our model using a temporally independent cohort rather than a spatially distinct dataset in this study. Although this temporal validation cohort provides valuable insight into model performance over time and helps assess potential time decay, it is not completely equivalent to traditional external validation across centres and regions and may limit the generalizability of the models. Therefore, future work will require multicentre and geographically diverse external validation to robustly establish the model’s generalizability across varied clinical settings and assess the usefulness of the online platform.

In conclusion, a prognostic model based on the RF algorithm was developed as a non-invasive and reliable method to assist clinicians in predicting the likelihood of recurrence after ESD in patients with SESCC. The model demonstrated good discrimination, calibration and interpretability and is accessible via an online platform to support individualized follow-up planning. Notably, LDL emerged as a key predictor, suggesting that lipid-related interventions may hold potential clinical value. Future work will focus on prospective multicentre validation, integration of multimodal data and evaluation of risk-guided strategies to improve patient outcomes.

figures.label: Figure 1.
figures.caption: Flowchart of the study. Sig: SESCC: superficial oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma; ESD: endoscopic submucosal dissection; RCS: restricted cubic spline; LASSO: the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator; RFE: recursive feature elimination; Logistic: logistic regression; XGBoost: extreme gradient boosting; LightGBM: light gradient boosting machine; RF: random forest; GBDT: gradient boosting decision tree; GNB: Gaussian Naïve Bayes; ROC: receiver operating characteristic; PR: precision-recall; DCA: decision curve analysis; SHAP: SHapley Additive exPlanations.

figures.label: Figure 2.
figures.caption: Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis of the dose-response relationship between various continuous variables and postoperative recurrence. Specific continuous variables include (A) biological age (BA), (B) fasting blood glucose (FBG) and (C) lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR).

figures.label: Figure 3.
figures.caption: Feature selection for predictive variables using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression algorithm and recursive feature elimination (RFE). (A) Path diagram and (B) cross-validation plot (1-SE criterion) for LASSO regression. The nine variables selected by LASSO was highlighted in bold. (C) Relationship between cross-validation accuracy and the number of variables. The dashed red line indicates the optimal subset (top 17 features). (D) Ranking of variable importance based on the optimal variable subset selected by RFE.

figures.label: Figure 4.
figures.caption: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis (A, D) and precision-recall curve analysis (B, E) for seven machine learning models in the training and internal test sets. (C) Decision curve analysis and (F) calibration curve analysis of seven models in the internal test set. Logistic: logistic regression; XGBoost: extreme gradient boosting; LightGBM: light gradient boosting machine; RF: random forest; GBDT: gradient boosting decision tree; GNB: Gaussian Naïve Bayes; MLP: Multilayer Perceptron.

figures.label: Figure 5.
figures.caption: ROC curve analysis of the Random Forest model for predicting recurrence risk in superficial oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SESCC) patients undergoing endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) in the temporal validation set. ROC: receiver operating characteristic.

figures.label: Figure 6.
figures.caption: Interpretation of Random Forest model features using the SHAP method. (A) SHAP summary bar plot, ranking features in descending order of mean SHAP values to assess their contributions to the model. (B) SHAP summary dot plot, displaying SHAP values along the x-axis to visualize the effect of each feature on model predictions. The colour gradient (purple to orange) represents feature values, and the distribution pattern indicates the influence direction and strength. (C) SHAP waterfall diagram, with the x-axis indicating the predicted value and the y-axis listing features along with their specific values. SHAP values are annotated for each feature, showing their respective positive or negative impact on the prediction result. This plot illustrates how the model predicts recurrence for the second superficial oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SESCC) patient by aggregating SHAP values. SHAP: SHapley Additive exPlanations.

figures.label: Figure 7.
figures.caption: Web-based platform for predicting recurrence in superficial oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SESCC) patients after endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) treatment. By inputting postoperative pathological data (tumour location, number of lesions, tumour differentiation and invasion depth) and preoperative laboratory indicators (LMR, PLR, LDL and BA), recurrence risk can be predicted. LMR: lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio; PLR: platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio; LDL: low-density lipoprotein; BA: biological age.
